title: Shinnecock Oyster Project
summary: The Shinnecock Oyster Project connects Shinnecock maritime knowledge, shellfish restoration, aquaculture training, environmental stewardship, and living Native continuity in Shinnecock Bay.
why_this_matters: Initiated in 1974 with the construction of a versatile tribal shellfish hatchery, the Shinnecock Oyster Project represents a modern revitalization of the Nation's long maritime heritage. By blending traditional ecological knowledge with contemporary aquaculture science, this ongoing initiative demonstrates how Indigenous communities actively adapt to environmental changes while pursuing economic self-determination.
introduction_content: The Shinnecock Oyster Project began in 1974 as a Shinnecock-led effort to restore shellfish production, create jobs, and reconnect aquaculture training with Shinnecock Bay. Supported by the New York Community Trust and training connected to the Lummi School of Aquaculture, the project joined modern hatchery methods with Shinnecock relationships to water, shellfish, labor, and stewardship. The original project ended in the late 1980s or early 1990s and was later revived as part of continuing work to care for the bay.
history_content:
1974 The Shinnecock Oyster Project began with support from the New York Community Trust and training models connected to the Lummi School of Aquaculture in Bellingham, Washington. Shinnecock participants explored hatchery methods, tray culture, bay chemistry and biology, oyster seed sources, and ways to replenish Shinnecock Bay after decades of shellfish decline caused by overharvesting, disease, oyster drills, starfish, and water-quality changes. 11977-1978 A mini-hatchery was built on the Reservation to test whether Shinnecock Bay could support shellfish life on a larger scale. The work proved grow-out methods, cultivated shellfish to market size, and helped make the case for a larger hatchery. 21979-1981 Two full production years produced millions of cultured oysters and seed clams. The work was described as a Shinnecock effort toward self-support through shellfish restoration, technical training, and local employment. 3Late 1980s-1990s The original oyster project was discontinued and later revived. The history of the project still matters because it links environmental restoration, Shinnecock foodways, economic self-determination, and responsibility to bay ecosystems. 4

1979 Shinnecock Oyster Project source

A photographed 1979 cover for The Shinnecock Tribe Oyster Project/Oyster Farming and Rafting Techniques, Shinnecock Bay documents the project as Shinnecock-led shellfish work connected to bay stewardship, economic development, and Native control of coastal knowledge.

Source: July 1979 project cover, project archive / Shinnecock Archaeology and History Drive folder.
preservation_content: Learning With Care: Shinnecock Bay and the Shinnecock Reservation remain living community landscapes. This oyster-restoration story stays with community history, environmental care, and already shared visitor context, rather than directing readers toward facility, equipment, or operational details.
